field_rule: Sheath BODY and MARGIN hair + hair-fringe true ligule + BEARDED primary branch axils + open large panicle; verify tiny 2–4 mm multi-flowered spikelets on a single mature specimen.

habit.reference: Flora confirms tufted perennial growth, small 2–4(–6)-flowered spikelets; existing airy habit provisional until more direct panicle review.

diagnostic_checks.look: Distinguish actual sheath BODY hair from collar hair
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew describes HIRSUTE (hairy) sheaths, including outer margins, and a HAIR-FRINGE true ligule. Do not substitute a few hairs at the ligule for a genuinely hairy sheath surface.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Mourning lovegrass generally has smooth sheaths with hairs mostly only at their mouths; plains lovegrass often has conspicuously hairy collars.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; sheath/hair role needs close same-stem image

diagnostic_checks.look: Look at the BEARDED axils of the open panicle
diagnostic_checks.check: A rather large ovate open 25–60 cm panicle, 15–25 cm broad, with tufts of hairs at primary branch axils and several thin spreading branches. The tuft occurs at the panicle branch insertion, not the basal leaf collar.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Mourning lovegrass also has some bearded panicle axils, but has very fine involute blades and much smaller/linear spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; hair length/branch insertion photograph still pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Dissect the tiny many-floret spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew's typical narrow compressed spikelets are only 2–4 mm long, about 1–1.2 mm wide and 2–6-flowered; paleas persist on the rachilla as some lemmas shed. Strong contrast with the larger, dense, many-flowered red/stinkgrass spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Red lovegrass spikelets are generally ~6–20 mm and at least 10-flowered; look at actual scale rather than reddish tint.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; no locally measured floral macro certified

field_rule: MOURNING LOVEGRASS = unusually thin leaves and airy but finer panicle. Confirm inward-rolled blade with live cross section.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending

head.reference: Open ovate-to-pyramidal panicle 18–28 cm, capillary flexuous branches and solitary pedicelled spikelets.

ligule.reference: Ligule a true hair fringe; upper sheath oral hairs may also be visible.

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the extraordinarily fine, often INROLLED blade
diagnostic_checks.check: GrassBase describes narrow often involute blades about 1–2 mm wide, with a generally smooth sheath surface but some hair at its mouth. A large hairy sheath surface should make you compare with E. hirsuta.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Bigtop lovegrass has much broader 4–8 mm blades and hairy sheaths; sand lovegrass also has narrow blades but different floral details.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; leaf cross-section and sheath close-up still needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Trace the fine flexuous branches in the diffuse panicle
diagnostic_checks.check: The loose ovate/pyramidal 18–28 cm panicle has capillary FLEXUOUS branches, often grouped at lower nodes and with bearded axils. Branches carry solitary pedicelled small spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Bigtop has a much larger 25–60 cm open head, while red lovegrass can have dense contracted spikelet clusters.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew and FNA; panicle alone not final ID

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the very narrow small spikelet and glumes
diagnostic_checks.check: Typical spikelets ~3–4.5 mm long by 0.5–1 mm wide, generally 5–7-flowered, with 0.6–1 mm lower glumes and 1.1–1.4 mm upper glumes. The ligule is a hair fringe, not the hairs atop the sheath.
diagnostic_checks.compare: E. hirsuta spikelets ~2–4 mm long but wider 1–1.2 mm; blades and sheath hairs reinforce the difference.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew typical source range; specimen photo and floret count pending

field_rule: Physical species-recognition evidence: reddish compressed many-flowered spikelets + real leaf sheath/collar, with oxylepis qualification on the Goldman macro references; do not substitute appearance for same-specimen microscopy.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending

ligule.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O’Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, user-provided monocots excerpt, uploaded PDF p. 196
ligule.reference: Regional subsp. oxylepis has very short ligule with a membranous base obscured by longer blade-base hairs; source-specific variation, not an assertion that every taxon shows same collar.

taxon_concept.source: Kew POWO accepted species and two accepted subspecies; FNA Eragrostis secundiflora regional account
taxon_concept.reference: Whole-species GrassBase account 10–24 florets; FNA description for US subsp. oxylepis 10–45; use no absolute floret-count filter without regionally resolved taxon concept.

diagnostic_checks.look: Count florets in the red compressed spikelets, not just red color
diagnostic_checks.check: GrassBase describes strongly compressed 6–20 mm long, 3–5 mm wide spikelets usually with 10–24 florets, clustered along relatively stiff panicle branches. Flora of North America describes up to 45 florets for regionally treated subsp. oxylepis; keep the concept difference visible.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Purple lovegrass usually has slender 5–7 mm, 7–11-flowered spikelets and a broadly open tumbling panicle; red-purple color is shared.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew whole-species versus FNA regional subsp. oxylepis ranges differ; no rigid number cutoff
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Eragrostis secundiflora; FNA regional account

diagnostic_checks.look: Open a spikelet to measure glumes and the red lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: Typical GrassBase lower glume 2.5–3 mm (one-veined), upper glume 3–4 mm; fertile lemma 1.6–2.4 mm, often red and three-veined with distinct lateral veins. Count florets and measure one mature spikelet from several heads.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Stinkgrass is usually glandular and annual, while red lovegrass is generally eglandular and perennial; both can have dense many-flowered spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: GrassBase-backed floral characters; photo and exact taxon concept needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Check true ligule against nearby long throat hairs
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew describes a hair-fringe ligule; the older North Central Texas treatment of subsp. OXYLEPIS describes a tiny membranous base obscured by longer sheath-throat hairs. Preserve both broad choices until a mm-scaled inner collar shows the tissue. Plants from the FNA region are generally subsp. oxylepis.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Hirsute lovegrass can have long hairs at the sheath mouth, but tiny spikelet size (2–4 mm) and fewer florets differs sharply.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Taxon concept and photo microscopy unresolved; do not label all red-flowered Eragrostis subsp. oxylepis without voucher
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Eragrostis secundiflora; FNA regional taxon concept

field_rule: Texas cupgrass: separate hair-FRINGE true LIGULE from hairy culm nodes; inspect the little CUP/RING just under a fallen spikelet (reduced lower glume fused to callus); check 4–10 upright fuzzy one-sided racemes and attached paired 3.6–4.2 mm spikelets. Do not certify from a fuzzy flowering head alone.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses

habit.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas p.198
habit.reference: Tufted 30–100 cm grass with dense soft pubescence; species-level true ligule still not verified.

ligule.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase Eriochloa sericea; Texas A&M Plants of Texas Rangelands
ligule.reference: Dense ring/fringe of straight hairs at inner blade/sheath junction; this is a true hair ligule, not a ciliate papery membrane, independently attested.

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine the ringlike CUP beneath the falling spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: The cup of Texas cupgrass is a globose CALLUS/cupule representing the lowest rachilla internode with the reduced, fused lower glume, directly below the spikelet. After spikelets fall, little cup rings may remain at their points of attachment.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Signalgrasses have developed lower glumes but do not create this same rounded ring/cup beneath each fuzzy spikelet.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase plus Texas A&M regionally checked; actual empty attachment photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the REAL hair-fringe ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: Texas A&M and Kew both describe a DENSE FRINGE/RING of straight hairs at the inside blade–sheath junction, rather than a distinct papery membranous flap. Distinguish it from hairy culm nodes.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum flowering heads can also have one-sided racemes but usually membranous inner ligules.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Two independent regional/GrassBase source checks; current source photo has not been validated for collar

diagnostic_checks.look: Count the fuzzy racemes and inspect actual fertile spikelets
diagnostic_checks.check: Usually 4–10 short, erect unilateral racemes about 1.5–3 cm; spikelets PAIRED, around 3.6–4.2 mm, ovate and covered with hairs; five-veined upper glume and five-veined lower sterile lemma. A perennial rooted TUFT has no long runners.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Brownseed signalgrass has smaller ~2.4–3 mm spikelets and a different developed lower glume, and Vaseygrass has many longer racemes.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase description; need two-face floral closeup and rooted perennial base

photos.label: HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS — green overlapping spikelets and hairy blade margin
photos.creator: Turner Brockman

field_rule: Compact white/purplish woolly heads on slender largely bare flowering culms ABOVE a low tuft of folded white-edged leaves; verify smooth short glumes versus a THREE-NERVED hairy one-awned lemma.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas p.198
head.reference: Short contracted 2–4 cm head bearing around 4–12 large multi-flowered spikelets; apparent fluffy look is not a true branching cloud.

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare pale short HEAD with low folded white-margined leaves
diagnostic_checks.check: Hairy woollygrass makes a compact dense clubby head usually ~2–5 cm, on slender almost leafless stems about 10–30 cm high. Basal narrow folded gray-green blades have distinctive white cartilaginous margins; not a broad feathery branching panicle.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Munroa fluffgrass hides its 1–5 spikelets within short leafy fascicles, rather than a short club on a relatively naked stalk.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Texas A&M + Kew source-backed; leaf margin and intact head photo need exact roles
diagnostic_checks.source: Texas A&M — Hairy Tridens / Erioneuron pilosum

diagnostic_checks.look: Count the MANY FLORETS and a single short awn in one spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew describes 7–18 fertile FLORETS within typically 12–19 mm hairy spikelets; each fertile lemma roughly 4.5–6 mm has three veins and ONE small awn (~1–2 mm) protruding between two tip lobes, not three full awns.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Munroa has 1–5 spikelets per leafy fascicle and usually about 6–12 florets within a 7–13 mm spikelet, but a genuine flowering attachment and floret details must be checked.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase + Texas A&M; actual 10–20x lemma apex and floret count pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Locate the true HAIR-fringe ligule at a real collar
diagnostic_checks.check: Hairy woollygrass has a hair-fringe ligule around 0.5 mm; long soft hairs across palea and lemma and sometimes the narrow basal blades do NOT replace the tiny inner ligule. Culms form perennial TUFTS, without stolons.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Slim tridens has narrow contracted panicle, but often longer panicle and a CILIATE MEMBRANE at collar rather than hair-only ligule.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew-backed, exact local collar and lemma macros pending

field_rule: Recognize the compact repeated flowering units and stiff perennial habit first; confirm actual inner lacerate ligule and the three-spikelet fascicle before making an anatomical ID claim. Buried scaly rhizomes are a valuable later tiebreaker versus curlymesquite's surface stolons.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses

head.reference: Dense multilateral false spike of close unilateral short racemes with triads: one fertile, two male. A false spike, not an unbranched true spike.

habit.reference: Short rhizomes from tufted perennial crowns; not surface stolons as in curlymesquite.

awns.reference: Glume projections usually only 1–2 mm; 'no conspicuous long awns' does not mean strictly awnless.

diagnostic_checks.look: Expose SHORT rhizomes of a stiff clumped perennial
diagnostic_checks.check: Tobosa has erect often stiff flowering culms ~30–50 cm, rough narrow leaves and SHORT underground rhizomes. The ligule is a torn/erose eciliate MEMBRANE ~1 mm, separate from hairs at culm nodes.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Curlymesquite is low turf with wirelike surface stolons rooting at leafy nodes and more flexible short flowering culms.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; rootstock and true collar photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Count repeated paired SEX structures within each triad
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew describes several close one-sided short racemes gathered into a FALSE multilateral spike; each raceme carries one CENTRAL bisexual fertile spikelet and TWO lateral largely staminate spikelets. Note the separate spikelet insertion points.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Curlymesquite also makes triads, so the triad verifies Hilaria structure rather than TOBOSA species; compare habit and full head.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew description and regional flora; mature triad dissection still needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the hard/glume projections rather than counting long awns
diagnostic_checks.check: Tobosa's short false-spike branches and triads have broad, irregularly shaped glumes; short projections may be 1–2 mm but it lacks prominent LONG lemma awns. A head without visible projections is not botanically awnless.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Curlymesquite also has short glume awns and triads but is stoloniferous; use a connected rooted specimen.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew species account; paired glume surfaces and true length at mm scale pending

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.224
head.reference: Narrow spike-like head; not truly a simple unbranched spike.

diagnostic_checks.look: Trace the long RUNNER and look for white hairy swollen nodes
diagnostic_checks.check: Vine mesquite has long vine-like creeping stolons, sometimes to 1–2 m, and can also have shallow rhizomes. At some nodes prominent tufts of long white hairs make the stem look fuzzy. Trace to a rooted shoot.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Curlymesquite also runs but forms shorter low carpet and its flowering units are three-spikelet Hilaria clusters; bermudagrass has digitate fingers.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew morphology and Oklahoma State field account; a photo of a white runner alone does not establish same plant

diagnostic_checks.look: Look at SHORT APPRESSED lateral branches in an upright narrow head
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew describes 1–4 appressed unilateral short racemes (~1–2 cm) on a 3–10(14) cm upright head; a spike-like silhouette is a CONTRACTED panicle, not one simple spike. Spikelets are individual OVAL BLUNT objects.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dallisgrass typically has longer separated branches and paired spikelets; curlymesquite has repeated spikelet triads.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase source checked; whole panicle and branching insertions needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Open a rounded 3.4–4 mm spikelet and true membrane
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew gives mostly 3.4–4 mm smooth obtuse spikelets, with a basal MALE floret (palea present) and hardened fertile upper lemma; lower glume about 0.9–1 spikelet length FIVE-veined, upper glume full length SEVEN-veined. True ligule an eciliate 1–2 mm membrane.
diagnostic_checks.compare: A typical Panicum/Dichanthelium can share a two-floret spikelet but head geometry and glume ratios differ; Hopia's rounded spikelets plus runners offer a combination.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew species morphology checked; dissection required, not confirmed in current two photos

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.205
head.reference: An open rice cutgrass panicle with slender branches and spikelets distributed toward tips; source also confirms creeping slender rhizomes.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.205
habit.reference: Rhizomatous wetland grass; foliage and cutting leaf edges can help confirmation.

diagnostic_checks.look: Handle the blade edge carefully for backward-pointing prickles
diagnostic_checks.check: Rice cutgrass has sharply SCABROUS leaf margins that catch when a finger moves toward the leaf base. In wet riparian habitat this is a useful vegetative clue; don't assume every rough wetland grass is Leersia.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Phragmites and other wetland grasses may have rough blades, but their spikelet floral construction differs.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA and wetlands flora support; use noninjurious loupe rather than dragging bare skin

diagnostic_checks.look: Dissect a mature compressed spikelet—both glumes are absent
diagnostic_checks.check: Rice cutgrass has a ONE-FLORET flattened spikelet, normally 3.5–5(6.5) mm, **no glumes**, and a five-veined strongly hairy/rough keel on its hardened lemma; palea nearly equal to lemma.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum may lack LOWER glume but has an UPPER glume and typically two florets, so 'glumeless' has different meaning here.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA plus USDA wetland guide; true lemma/palea photo needs 10–20×

diagnostic_checks.look: Search upper leaf sheaths for a hidden panicle
diagnostic_checks.check: Perennial, rhizomatous rice cutgrass can have an OPEN 10–20 cm panicle or reduced CLEISTOGAMOUS (selfing) panicles partly/fully enclosed in upper leaf sheaths. Check rooted runners and hidden flowers before marking 'no head'.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Green sprangletop hides similar selfing structures in LOWER leaf sheaths, but has multiple florets and glumes; they differ substantially.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA wetland biology; upper-sheath observation and root connection pending

field_rule: NEVER certify a root-to-panicle connection, true ligule measurement, or 0.5 mm paired lemma teeth from photographs that do not show those structures plainly.

head.reference: Narrow erect or tip-nodding panicle but not perfectly cylindrical, awns geniculate about 8–12 mm.

diagnostic_checks.look: Trace the entire narrow FLOWERING PANICLE and true collar
diagnostic_checks.check: Ozarkgrass is an ANNUAL with a narrow but not perfectly cylindrical erect or slightly tip-nodding flowering head. The TRUE ligule is a roughly 1–2 mm **LACERATE-CILIATE MEMBRANE**, not long collar bristles; a mature rooted base confirms annual life cycle.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Pine muhly forms a much taller perennial tuft and narrowly contracted head but has short/absent rather than 8–11 mm bent lemma awns.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew / North Central Texas flora sources, exact field-rootstock photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Count glume veins and the one-floret spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: A 3.5–4 mm LATERALLY compressed spikelet has one fertile floret and a sterile rachilla extension; both similar stiff persistent glumes are ~3–5-veined and roughly reach the florets. Do not mistake an empty extension for a second developed floret.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Nassella has one floret and long awn too, but typically different sharp callus/lemma crown and glume form.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; mm-scaled closeup of BOTH glumes plus rachilla extension needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the BENT single awn behind two tiny lemma teeth
diagnostic_checks.check: The ~3.5–4 mm three-veined fertile lemma has two shallow terminal teeth and ONE twisted, geniculate awn usually 8–11(12) mm, rising from the back near the lemma apex, not three awns from the floret tip.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Aristida threeawns carry 3 distinct lemma awns; Erioneuron pilosum has only 1–2 mm awns on a MULTIFLORET spikelet.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase and regional flora checked; true lemma-awn origin photo unverified

diagnostic_checks.look: Look inside the 4–10 mm membrane and narrow rolled leaf
diagnostic_checks.check: Pine muhly forms a densely rooted tuft without rhizomes, with stiff involute ~1–2 mm blades and a firm pointed/lacerate MEMBRANE ligule 4–10 mm. Expose actual crown; a single cut leaf doesn't prove it lacks rhizomes.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Aparejo has long slender scaly rhizomes and only about a 0.5 mm membrane; nimblewill is stoloniferous and has a tiny ~0.5 mm membrane.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA description checked, connected crown and collar closeup pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Muhlenbergia dubia

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine the NARROW erect gray-green panicle
diagnostic_checks.check: Contracted 10–40 cm long, only 0.6–2.4 cm wide, stiff branching head; spikelets line branches almost to their base. It is not a soft, broad, open seep-muhly cloud.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Lindheimer muhly may also form a narrow panicle but has generally broader folded basal blades and often 8–15 mm ligules.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; dried panicle may compress more, exact field photo not certified
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Muhlenbergia dubia

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure mature spikelet, glumes, and a possibly ABSENT awn
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA reports ~3.8–5 mm single-floret spikelets; equal one-veined glumes usually 2–3 mm; lemma body 3.8–5 mm, smooth below and rougher at tip, either AWNLESS or with a straight awn up to ~6 mm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Canyon hybrid has shorter ~2–2.5 mm lemma and a tiny central awn between teeth; seep muhly has a more open head.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source, short-awn vs no-obvious-awn appearance preserved; actual dissection pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Muhlenbergia dubia

field_rule: Start with an erect COMPACT basal tuft of extremely thin, often inward-rolled blades, generally smaller than Lindheimer muhly. At bloom, confirm the delicate OPEN branching panicle, often reddish, with one-flowered awned spikelets. Inspect the membranous ligule and the small leaf width on a fresh blade under magnification; color alone is not diagnostic.

awns.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O’Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, user-provided monocots excerpt, uploaded PDF p. 212
awns.reference: Lemma awn 0.5–4(–7) mm; short awns may look inconspicuous in whole-head field view, the long end may be visible in close-up; variable choice states retained.

diagnostic_checks.look: Open a TRUE membrane and look for rolled threadlike blades
diagnostic_checks.check: Seep muhly has very slender, inward-rolled 1–2 mm leaves, and a membranous often ragged ligule generally 2–4 mm (occasionally 9). Tuft is usually much finer than Lindheimer muhly.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Lindheimer has wider folded blades and a conspicuous 8–15 mm inner ligule; young plants overlap in overall size.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew-backed; current photo set does not certify ligule or blade cross-section

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow the airy spreading flowering BRANCHES
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew describes an open ovate panicle about 10–20(30) cm long and 4–10(15) cm wide, with stiff outward branches. Red or pink color is variable and fades with season.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Lindheimer is normally relatively narrow and heavily flowered; Canyon hybrid is often a less diffuse 18–40 cm head with ascending branches.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew species description; flowering-stage and autumn dry-head photo QA pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure one fertile spikelet and the short glumes
diagnostic_checks.check: One fertile floret per 3.5–5 mm spikelet. Its two similar ONE-veined glumes are only ~1–2.5(3) mm, noticeably shorter than the spikelet; three-veined lemma usually with one fine awn ~0.5–3(6) mm. These awns may be hard to see in general head photos.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Lindheimer glumes reach close to the floret tip; Canyon hybrid glumes ~2–2.5 and 0.5–2 mm lemma awn. Many dimensions overlap.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; need actual glume/lemma separation with scale, not head color

awns.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O’Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, user-provided monocots excerpt, uploaded PDF p. 214
awns.reference: Short/narrow contracted panicle; decumbent stems ROOT AT LOWER NODES; lemma awn 1.5–5 mm (visible at closer range, often not conspicuous in distant whole-head photo). Surface mat recorded without asserting verified root nodes in photos.

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow the ABOVEGROUND stolon to its rooting nodes
diagnostic_checks.check: Nimblewill is a weak mat-forming PERENNIAL, many slender low stems branching and rooting at low nodes. Its surface stolons are NOT subterranean rhizomes. Fall/winter mats may turn brown; dormant mats alone are ambiguous.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Aparejo (*M. utilis*) spreads by SCALY underground rhizomes and has much shorter 1–4 cm narrow heads.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Ohio State and Iowa Extension; attached rooted runner photo still needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Open the minute erose membrane in the leaf collar
diagnostic_checks.check: True ligule is a very short ragged/ciliolate MEMBRANE typically ~0.2–0.5 mm, partly hidden by long hairs at the blade/sheath mouth. Faint white collar hairs alone do not prove ligule type.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Aparejo has an eciliate ~0.5 mm membrane; slender stolon vs rhizome plus floral anatomy are stronger.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Ohio State; actual 10–20x blade junction and nearby throat hair closeup pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect a solitary narrow spikelet with extremely SMALL glumes
diagnostic_checks.check: Terminal/axillary narrow contracted panicles often 5–15 cm long; single-floret spikelets about 1.8–2.8 mm. LOWER glume minute or absent and upper glume only ~0.1–0.3 mm; lemma around 2 mm usually with a 1.5–5 mm awn.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Aparejo has BOTH glumes clearly present at ~0.6–1(1.3) mm, and an awnless 1.6–2 mm lemma. Don't treat awn visibility in distant photos as proof.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Ohio State and Go Botany measurements; exact same-spikelet glume view pending
